entry.title: From SpliceAI to SpliceAI2: the technical toolbox of modern sequence-to-splicing models

link.title: From SpliceAI to SpliceAI2: the technical toolbox of modern sequence-to-splicing models

entry.content:
RNA splicing is one of the cleanest examples of a sequence-to-function problem in biology. The input is a stretch of genomic DNA. The output is the set of introns that get removed, how often each one is removed, and which full-length mRNA isoforms are produced. Everything in between, including the spliceosome, hundreds of RNA-binding proteins, co-transcriptional kinetics and chromatin, is hidden from the model.

Since SpliceAI (2019), a whole family of deep learning models has tried to learn this mapping directly from sequence. In October 2026, Illumina released SpliceAI2, described in the manuscript “A unified framework for quantitative splicing and transcript prediction” (Jaganathan, Chen, Liu, Zhang et al.). On paper it is a large step: it reads about 200 kb of sequence, predicts splice site usage, splice junction usage and complete transcripts, and it is trained on 314,745 RNA-seq samples from ten mammalian species.

The question this post asks is not only:

How accurate is SpliceAI2?

but rather:

Which technical choices make a modern splicing model work,
and how do SpliceAI2 and its recent peers differ in those choices?

I first set up the prediction problem, then walk through the lineage of recent models, and then take SpliceAI2 apart component by component: backbone, output heads, the splice graph and its dynamic programming loss, training targets, optimization, variant scoring and tissue conditioning. At the end I summarize the shared design space and what still seems to be missing.

1. Splicing prediction as a hierarchy of outputs

For a gene with genomic sequence $x \in {A,C,G,T}^L$, splicing can be described at several levels of resolution. Each level is a different prediction target.

Level 1: splice site identity. For every position $p$, is it a donor (5’ splice site), an acceptor (3’ splice site), or neither?

\[y_p \in \{\text{none}, \text{donor}, \text{acceptor}\}\]

Level 2: splice site usage. How often is position $p$ used as a donor or acceptor?

\[u^{d}_p, \; u^{a}_p \in [0, 1]\]

Level 3: splice junction usage. How often is the intron from donor $i$ to acceptor $j$ removed?

\[J_{ij} \in [0,1], \quad i < j\]

Level 4: transcript usage. What fraction of the gene’s mRNA molecules follow a specific intron chain $T$?

\[p(T), \quad \sum_{T} p(T) = 1\]

These levels are not independent. A junction needs a used donor and a used acceptor. A transcript is a compatible chain of non-overlapping junctions. Most of the history of splicing models can be read as a climb up this hierarchy:

SpliceAI (2019)          → level 1 (site identity)
Pangolin, DeltaSplice    → level 2 (site usage, quantitative)
Splam, AlphaGenome       → level 3 (junctions, pairwise)
SpliceAI2 (2026)         → level 4 (full transcripts), trained end-to-end on levels 2–4

For variant interpretation, every level gives a delta. If $f$ is the model and $x^{\text{ref}}, x^{\text{alt}}$ are the reference and alternate sequences, the variant effect is

\[\Delta = f(x^{\text{alt}}) - f(x^{\text{ref}})\]

computed at the relevant positions, pairs, or transcripts. The finer the level, the closer the prediction is to the biological consequence (for example a frameshift transcript or an exon skip) rather than a proxy for it.

2. The lineage: what each recent model contributed

Before going into SpliceAI2, it helps to see what each recent model added to the toolbox. I focus on technical ideas rather than leaderboard numbers.

2.1 SpliceAI (2019): long context with dilated residual convolutions

SpliceAI established the basic recipe:

  • one-hot encoded DNA input;
  • a deep stack of residual blocks with dilated 1D convolutions, so the receptive field grows quickly with depth;
  • the largest model (SpliceAI-10k) sees 5,000 nt on each side of each position;
  • a per-position 3-class softmax (none / acceptor / donor);
  • labels from annotated GENCODE transcripts;
  • a variant delta score: the largest change in donor or acceptor probability within a ±50 nt window.

Its central lesson was that long-range context matters. Splice site choice depends on exon definition, intron length, competing sites and distal regulatory elements, not only on the local 9-mer or 23-mer motifs used by MaxEntScan.

Its central limitation was that it learned annotation, a binary property, rather than usage, a quantitative property. A rarely used cryptic site and a constitutive site both look like “1” or “0”.

2.2 Pangolin (2022): quantitative and tissue-aware

Pangolin kept a SpliceAI-like dilated convolutional backbone but changed the targets:

  • trained on RNA-seq from four species (human, rhesus macaque, mouse, rat) and four tissues (heart, liver, brain, testis);
  • per tissue, it predicts both the probability that a site is spliced and its splice site usage (SSU), a continuous value;
  • tissues are handled as separate output heads in a multitask setup.

The new tools are RNA-seq-derived quantitative targets and multi-species training as data augmentation. Orthologous genes across mammals share a splicing code but differ in sequence, which acts like natural mutagenesis.

2.3 DeltaSplice (2024): bigger context and reference-informed prediction

DeltaSplice extended the receptive field to about 30 kb, with a residual CNN core and roughly an order of magnitude more parameters than SpliceAI. Its distinctive idea is a dual-sequence mode. To predict usage for a mutated sequence, the model also receives the reference sequence together with its measured usage, and predicts the target relative to that anchor.

single mode:  x            → usage
dual mode:    (x_ref, u_ref, x_alt) → usage(x_alt)

This is a form of conditioning on a known baseline. Variant effect prediction becomes closer to predicting a difference than predicting two absolute values and subtracting them.

2.4 Splam (2024): thinking in pairs

Splam, from the Salzberg and Pertea groups, is built for spliced alignment rather than variant scoring, but it made an important conceptual move. Instead of scoring donors and acceptors independently, it scores a donor and an acceptor together as a junction. The input is a short window around each end of the intron, concatenated, passed through a residual convolutional network. This allows Splam to filter spurious junctions from RNA-seq alignments.

The tool here is pairwise prediction. A junction is a property of two positions, not one.

2.5 SpliceTransformer (2024): attention for tissue-specific splicing

SpliceTransformer (SpTransformer) adds self-attention on top of convolutional features to predict tissue-specific splice site usage across many tissues, and applies the model to ClinVar variants to link tissue-specific splicing changes to disease. It represents the trend of moving from pure CNNs to hybrid conv–attention models for long sequences.

2.6 AlphaGenome (2025–2026): splicing inside a general sequence-to-function model

AlphaGenome from Google DeepMind is not a splicing-specific model. It takes 1 Mb of DNA and predicts thousands of genomic tracks (expression, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, contact maps, and more) with a U-Net-like architecture: convolutional downsampling, a transformer at coarse resolution, and upsampling back to base-pair resolution.

For splicing, it has three relevant output types:

  • splice site classification;
  • splice site usage;
  • splice junctions, predicted by a dedicated pairwise head that combines embeddings of candidate donor and acceptor positions and outputs junction read counts per tissue.

So AlphaGenome also reaches level 3 of the hierarchy, and it brings massive multimodal supervision. For variant scoring, its documentation recommends a composite score that adds the splice site, splice site usage and scaled junction effects.

2.7 OpenSpliceAI (2025): retrainable infrastructure

OpenSpliceAI is a PyTorch reimplementation of SpliceAI with a modular training pipeline. It reproduces SpliceAI’s accuracy and makes it practical to retrain on new species or annotations. Its contribution is infrastructure, not architecture. This matters because many of the later gains come from data and targets, which only help if retraining is cheap.

A side note: Kuan-Hao Chao, first author of Splam and OpenSpliceAI, is also a co-author of SpliceAI2. The pairwise-junction idea and the retrainable-pipeline idea both reappear in SpliceAI2.

3. SpliceAI2 at a glance

SpliceAI2 combines most of the ideas above and adds one new piece: a structured transcript layer. At a high level:

196,608 bp DNA + species one-hot
        ↓
dense projection to 256 channels
        ↓
20 multi-scale MetaFormer blocks (depthwise dilated conv + FFN)
        ↓                                   ↓
per-block splice site heads          per-block query/key heads
(averaged → sigmoid)                 on top-1,024 candidate sites
        ↓                                   ↓
donor/acceptor usage                 pairwise junction usage
over central 65,536 bp               (1,024 × 1,024, upper triangle)
        ↓                                   ↓
        └───────────── splice graph ────────┘
                         ↓
       dynamic programming (forward algorithm / Viterbi)
                         ↓
         transcript distribution and top-k isoforms

Key numbers from the methods:

Component SpliceAI2 setting
Input length 196,608 bp (65,536 bp of flank on each side of the predicted window)
Output window central 65,536 positions
Input channels 4 (nucleotide) + 10 (species one-hot)
Backbone 20 MetaFormer blocks, 256 channels
Candidate splice sites for junctions top 1,024 positions
Parameters about 13M
Short-read data 314,745 RNA-seq samples, 10 mammals, ~67M junctions before filtering
Long-read data 330 ENCODE samples (189 human, 141 mouse)
Training 50 epochs, Muon + AdamW, bf16, 4×H100, ensemble of 2

Notice the parameter count. At about 13M parameters, SpliceAI2 is small by modern standards, much smaller than AlphaGenome. Most of the improvement comes from data scale, target design and output structure, not from model size.

4. The backbone: a multi-scale convolutional MetaFormer

4.1 MetaFormer blocks

A MetaFormer is the abstract transformer skeleton with the attention layer replaced by any “token mixer”:

\[h' = h + \mathrm{TokenMixer}(\mathrm{Norm}(h)), \qquad h'' = h' + \mathrm{ChannelMixer}(\mathrm{Norm}(h'))\]

In SpliceAI2:

  • Token mixer: batch normalization, then a depthwise convolution with kernel size 5 and a dilation rate that doubles every two blocks;
  • Channel mixer: batch normalization, then a feed-forward network with expansion ratio 4 and ReLU.

This is essentially a ConvNeXt-style block for 1D sequences. Depthwise convolutions mix information only along the sequence, and the FFN mixes only across channels. That separation is cheaper than a dense convolution and works well with the transformer-style residual layout.

4.2 Multi-scale processing: pooling inside each block

The second ingredient is less common. Each block is preceded by average pooling and followed by linear upsampling back to base-pair resolution, and the pooling factor doubles every four blocks.

block b:  h  → AvgPool(factor_b) → MetaFormer block → Upsample(factor_b) → h_b
factor_b: 1,1,1,1, 2,2,2,2, 4,4,4,4, 8,8,8,8, 16,16,16,16   (doubling every 4 blocks)

(The schedule above is illustrative. The paper states that the factor doubles every four blocks, but does not give the starting value.)

The dilation also doubles every two blocks. The two mechanisms multiply, so the deep blocks see very long ranges at low cost. Pooling by 16 means one convolution tap spans 16 bp, and with a large dilation a kernel of size 5 can span thousands of bases.

Why not a transformer over 196 kb? Self-attention over about $2 \times 10^5$ tokens at base resolution is very expensive. AlphaGenome solves this by downsampling heavily before attention. SpliceAI2 avoids global attention altogether in the backbone. Splicing is dominated by local motifs plus a few long-range dependencies, which suits a convolution-only design with an exponentially growing receptive field.

4.3 Deep supervision through per-block heads

The splice site output is not read from the last layer only. Each of the 20 blocks has its own dense head. The outputs are cropped to the central 65,536 positions and averaged:

\[\hat{u}_p = \sigma\left( \frac{1}{20} \sum_{b=1}^{20} W_b \, h_b(p) \right) \in [0,1]^2\]

where the two channels are donor and acceptor usage.

This has several effects:

  • shallow blocks capture local motif strength (the GT/AG dinucleotides, polypyrimidine tract, branch point);
  • deep blocks capture long-range context (exon definition, competing sites);
  • averaging in logit space makes the final prediction a sum of evidence across scales;
  • every block receives a direct gradient, which stabilizes training of a 20-block network.

The same per-block averaging is used in the junction head.

5. The junction head: attention scores as edges

5.1 Selecting candidate sites

A 65,536 × 65,536 junction matrix would have more than 4 billion entries. SpliceAI2 avoids it by first selecting the 1,024 positions with the highest predicted splice site usage, taking the maximum of donor and acceptor usage, and sorting them by coordinate. Junctions are only predicted among these candidates.

5.2 Bilinear scoring with genomic RoPE

For each block $b$, the features at the 1,024 candidate positions are layer-normalized and projected to queries and keys. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) are applied using the genomic coordinates of the sites, not their rank among candidates:

\[s^{(b)}_{ij} = \frac{\left\langle \mathrm{RoPE}(q_b(h_b(i)), \, x_i), \; \mathrm{RoPE}(k_b(h_b(j)), \, x_j) \right\rangle}{\sqrt{d}}\]

The lower triangle including the diagonal is masked, so only $i < j$ (upstream donor, downstream acceptor on the sense strand) survives. The junction usage is

\[\hat{J}_{ij} = \sigma\left( \frac{1}{20} \sum_{b=1}^{20} s^{(b)}_{ij} \right)\]

This is attention without the softmax and without values. The query–key dot product is used directly as an edge score. RoPE makes the score depend on the relative distance $x_j - x_i$, which is exactly the intron length. Intron length is a strong biological prior for junction choice: very short introns are disfavored, and exon definition operates over typical exon sizes.

Note the sigmoid, not a softmax. Each junction is an independent Bernoulli-style prediction of usage. A donor can be paired with several acceptors at different levels, which is how alternative splicing appears in the data.

5.3 Teacher forcing for candidate selection

During training, the 1,024 candidate sites are taken from the ground-truth splice site usage, not from predictions. The paper gives two reasons:

  • early in training, predictions are arbitrary, and candidates chosen from them would be meaningless;
  • it avoids ever materializing the full junction matrix.

This is the same logic as teacher forcing in sequence models: decouple the selection step from the learning step until the model is good enough to select for itself.

6. The splice graph and dynamic programming: the key new idea

6.1 Transcripts as paths

SpliceAI2 combines site and junction predictions into a splice graph:

  • nodes are the candidate splice sites, ordered along the gene;
  • a directed edge $i \to j$ represents an intron from donor $i$ to acceptor $j$;
  • consecutive sites are also joined by an exon continuation edge with weight 0.

For implementation, node weights are folded into edges. The weight of an intron edge is the sum of three logits:

\[w_{ij} = \mathrm{logit}(\hat{u}^{d}_i) + \mathrm{logit}(\hat{J}_{ij}) + \mathrm{logit}(\hat{u}^{a}_j)\]

A transcript $T$ is a path through the graph: a chain of non-overlapping introns separated by exonic stretches. Its score is

\[s(T) = \sum_{(i,j) \in T} w_{ij}\]

and the model’s transcript distribution is a Gibbs distribution over all paths:

\[p(T) = \frac{e^{s(T)}}{Z}, \qquad Z = \sum_{T' \in \mathcal{T}} e^{s(T')}\]

This is a linear-chain / semi-Markov conditional random field over splice sites, with neural potentials. It connects deep splicing models back to classical gene finders such as GENSCAN and to recent hybrid models like Tiberius and Helixer, which combine neural networks with HMMs.

6.2 Training with the forward algorithm

Long-read RNA-seq gives an observed transcript distribution $q(T)$. The transcript loss is cross-entropy:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{tx}} = -\sum_{T} q(T) \log p(T) = -\sum_{T} q(T) \, s(T) + \log Z\]

The first term only involves observed transcripts, so it is cheap. The second term sums over an exponentially large set of paths. It is computed exactly with a forward recursion. Let $\alpha_j$ be the total exponentiated score of all paths through the first $j$ sites:

\[\alpha_{j+1} = \underbrace{\alpha_j}_{\text{exon continuation}} + \sum_{i \le j} \alpha_i \, e^{w_{i,j+1}}\]

This takes $O(N^2)$ time in the number of candidate sites, which is affordable for $N = 1{,}024$. Because every step is differentiable, the gradient of $\log Z$ flows back through the junction head and the splice site head into the backbone. This means transcript-level supervision shapes site-level and junction-level predictions.

In practice, the transcript loss is weighted by $10^{-5}$ because $\log Z$ is numerically large compared with the per-position BCE losses.

6.3 Decoding with Viterbi and k-best paths

At inference, the most likely transcript is found by replacing the sum with a max:

\[\beta_{j+1} = \max\left( \beta_j, \; \max_{i \le j} \left( \beta_i + w_{i,j+1} \right) \right)\]

with back-pointers to recover the path. Replacing the max with a k-max gives the $k$ best transcripts in one pass, which is how the paper shows the top three isoforms of a held-out gene (NOL12).

On held-out genes on chromosomes 21 and 22, SpliceAI2 exactly reconstructs the most abundant transcript for 82% of genes. Without long-read supervision, the figure is 78%; with the site output alone (the “1D” setting in Fig. 1c), it is 77%. The headline is that short-read data already gets most of the way, because good site and junction potentials already imply good paths. Long reads add global consistency.

6.4 Why this matters

Previous models give you site and junction scores, and building isoforms from them is left to the user, usually with heuristics. SpliceAI2 makes the isoform an explicit latent structure with a proper likelihood. This makes several things possible:

  • exact marginal probabilities of transcripts;
  • a principled way to combine short-read (local) and long-read (global) supervision in one objective;
  • direct prediction of the transcript consequence of a variant, for example an exon skip or intron retention that leads to a frameshift.

In my view, this is the most important technical contribution of the paper.

7. Training targets: normalization and the cube root

7.1 From junction counts to usage

The short-read targets come from STAR junction counts summed across all samples of a species. Within each gene:

  • donor usage at $p$: sum of counts of all junctions using $p$ as donor;
  • acceptor usage at $p$: sum of counts of all junctions using $p$ as acceptor;
  • both are divided by the largest such count in the gene;
  • junction counts are divided by the same value.

So usage is relative to the most-used site of the gene, not a PSI with a local denominator. This makes the targets comparable across a gene and keeps the site and junction outputs on the same scale.

7.2 Cube root: making rare sites count

All usage values are then passed through a cube root:

\[\tilde{u} = u^{1/3}\]
raw usage $u$ target $u^{1/3}$
0.001 0.10
0.01 0.22
0.1 0.46
1.0 1.00

Without the transform, a site used 0.1% of the time contributes almost nothing to a BCE loss. After it, it becomes a clear signal at 0.1. The ablation in the paper attributes much of SpliceAI2’s gain to these rarely used sites. Their characterization depends on the very deep coverage obtained by pooling 314,745 samples, and their contribution to training depends on the cube root.

This links directly to the variant problem. A cryptic splice site activated by a rare variant often looks like a site that the reference sequence uses at a very low level. Learning the low-usage tail of the reference transcriptome is learning the space of cryptic sites.

7.3 Losses

The full pretraining objective is

\[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}^{\text{site}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{BCE}}^{\text{junction}} + 10^{-5} \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{tx}}\]

with BCE against soft targets (the cube-rooted usage), restricted to positions within genes.

8. Data and optimization

8.1 Data curation at scale

The short-read data come from recount3 (human, mouse) and the NCBI SRA (eight other mammals: chimpanzee, baboon, two macaques, cow, sheep, pig, rat). Two details stand out:

  • projects were classified as bulk, single-cell or ambiguous by Llama 3.3, using their titles and abstracts, and only bulk RNA-seq was kept. This is a nice example of using an LLM as a cheap metadata curator;
  • reads were mapped with STAR using annotation-free indices, so junction discovery is not biased toward known annotation.

Junctions were then restricted to protein-coding genes, required at least one annotated end, and required the gene to reach at least 1,000 junction reads at its top junction.

Long-read data come from all ENCODE long-read samples. Isoforms were merged by intron chain, because the model only predicts splicing, not transcription start or polyadenylation sites.

8.2 Species as an input, not a head

The species is provided as a one-hot input channel, broadcast along the sequence. This differs from Pangolin’s per-species output heads. The backbone sees which genome it is reading and can adjust, while all parameters remain shared.

8.3 Optimizer and schedule

  • Muon for feed-forward weight matrices, AdamW for everything else;
  • learning rate $10^{-3}$, dropped to $10^{-4}$ after 40 of 50 epochs, weight decay 0.01;
  • bfloat16 mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, batch size 4 per device on 4 H100 GPUs;
  • initialization from $\mathcal{N}(0, 0.01^2)$, biases at zero;
  • two models trained identically form the final ensemble.

Muon orthogonalizes the update of each weight matrix (via Newton–Schulz iterations) and has become popular in LLM training. Seeing it in a genomics model is a sign that genomic deep learning is now borrowing optimization tricks directly from the LLM stack.

8.4 Avoiding leakage

Human chromosomes 21 and 22 are held out. For the transcript reconstruction benchmark, the authors train human-only models, because orthologous genes from other species would leak the held-out human gene structure. This is a subtle point: multi-species training is fine for variant effects, but it can inflate reference-sequence benchmarks.

9. Variant scoring: getting the details right

Scoring a variant sounds simple: run reference and alternate, subtract. With a candidate-selection step, it is not.

If the reference and alternate alleles were scored independently, and each ensemble member chose its own top 1,024 sites, the junction matrices would not be aligned. A variant that creates a new site would put it in one candidate set but not the other.

SpliceAI2’s solution:

  1. run both alleles (196,608 bp centred on the variant) through the backbone of both ensemble members;
  2. average donor and acceptor usage over the ensemble;
  3. select one shared candidate set: the 1,024 positions with the largest usage, maximized over donor/acceptor and over both alleles;
  4. compute junctions for both alleles on these shared sites, averaged over the ensemble;
  5. report donor gain/loss, acceptor gain/loss and junction gain/loss, keeping the ten largest effects per category.

The summary score is the maximum across donor gain, donor loss, acceptor gain and acceptor loss. Interestingly, junction gain/loss effects were found to give no net improvement to the summary score and are kept only for visualization. Even though the model predicts junctions well, the site-level delta remains the most robust single number for prioritization.

10. Tissue-specific splicing: conditioning on RBP expression

10.1 Tissue as a biological signature, not an ID

Pangolin and AlphaGenome represent tissues as output heads or tracks. Each tissue gets its own parameters. SpliceAI2 instead fine-tunes a model that takes the tissue as an input vector: the expression of 147 RNA-binding proteins (79 from RBPmap, 68 from oRNAment), as log2 TMM-CPM from GTEx, divided by 20 and broadcast along the sequence.

\[f_\theta(x, \; r) \rightarrow \text{tissue-specific junction usage}, \qquad r \in \mathbb{R}^{147}\]

This changes the meaning of “tissue”. It becomes a point in a regulator space, and the model learns how sequence motifs interact with regulator abundance. It also means the model can, in principle, be queried with any RBP vector, including disease states or perturbations that it never saw as named tissues.

10.2 Architecture of the fine-tuning model

The pretrained MetaFormer blocks are kept, and two kinds of modules are added:

Signature injection modules, before each of the 20 blocks:

  • bidirectional FiLM (bi-FiLM): the RBP signature modulates the sequence features through feature-wise scale and shift, and the sequence stream also modulates the signature stream;
  • a convolutional block with batch norm and a squeeze-and-excitation gate;
  • the result is scaled by a learnable scalar and added residually to the sequence embedding.

The learnable residual scale makes the injection start near zero, so fine-tuning begins from the pretrained model’s behaviour.

A three-layer cross-attention decoder:

  • queries are sequence embeddings at anchor splice sites, plus a learned tissue embedding;
  • RoPE with $\theta = 10^5$ (long wavelengths for kilobase distances), linear relative position biases and QK-normalization;
  • output logits are soft-capped as $10 \tanh(x/10)$ for stability;
  • for each anchor, partners on the wrong side (upstream of a donor, downstream of an acceptor) are masked, and a softmax over positions gives the distribution of junction usage for that anchor.

Note the switch from sigmoid to softmax. In pretraining, junction usage is normalized per gene. In the tissue model, it is anchor-based: for a given donor, what fraction of its junctions go to each acceptor? This is essentially PSI3/PSI5, the quantity that changes between tissues.

10.3 Losses for differences, not only values

Fine-tuning uses three losses:

  • cross-entropy on anchor-based junction usage;
  • weighted BCE for donor/acceptor classification;
  • an MSE contrastive loss on pairwise tissue differences: the predicted difference between tissues A and B should match the measured difference.

The third loss is important. Most junctions are constitutive and identical across tissues. A model can achieve a low absolute error by ignoring tissues entirely. A loss on differences forces the model to spend capacity on the part of the signal that is actually tissue-specific.

10.4 What it can and cannot do

Across 48 GTEx tissues and about 14.7 million tissue-pair comparisons on held-out chromosomes, predicted and observed differences correlate at Pearson $r = 0.44$, rising to 0.58 for cerebellum vs blood. Two technical findings are worth noting:

  • fine-tuning from the pretrained model clearly beats training from scratch, so the shared splicing code transfers;
  • the RBP signature only marginally beats a one-hot tissue ID. The biological representation is more interpretable and more flexible, but not much more accurate on GTEx.

The flexibility is shown by counterfactual conditioning. With identical DNA input, swapping in the RBP vector of SF3B1-mutant vs wild-type uveal melanoma, or of myotonic dystrophy at different MBNL1 levels, reproduces disease-associated splicing differences in held-out genes. In silico mutagenesis recovers RBFOX, QKI, HNRNPA2B1 and MBNL1 motifs, and the strength of these motifs tracks the expression of the corresponding RBP across tissues.

The honest limitation: for tissue-specific variant effects, the tissue model adds nothing beyond knowing the reference splicing levels in each tissue, the same conclusion reached by ABSplice. In other words, the model knows which tissues use a junction differently, but not yet how a variant’s effect depends on tissue beyond that.

11. Benchmarks

All numbers below are from the SpliceAI2 manuscript, with essential splice dinucleotide variants excluded. They are reported by the developers; independent evaluation will matter.

Benchmark Metric SpliceAI Pangolin AlphaGenome SpliceAI2
GTEx GT/AG cryptic sites (4,545 vs 573,967) auPRC 0.66 0.56 0.54 0.77
GTEx GT/AG cryptic usage Spearman ρ 0.45 0.47 0.41 0.63

UK Biobank plasma protein Pearson r −0.463 −0.475 −0.481 −0.504

Some observations:

  • the largest gain is on cryptic site detection, especially for deep intronic variants, which fits the cube-root and data-scale explanation in Section 7;
  • AlphaGenome is strongest among baselines on the sQTL tasks, which involve common, often regulatory, variants;
  • on the MPRA, all models are closer together, suggesting that exon-skipping in reporter constructs is a different and harder regime;
  • AlphaGenome scores depended strongly on scorer configuration (40 configurations tested). A single generalist model exposes many possible scores, and choosing one is part of the evaluation.

In the Genomics England rare disease cohort, SpliceAI2-prioritized cryptic splice variants account for about 15% of the excess genetic burden, and half of them lie more than 50 bp into introns, outside typical exome capture.

12. The shared design space

Placing all the models side by side, the choices fall along a few axes.

Axis SpliceAI Pangolin DeltaSplice Splam AlphaGenome SpliceAI2
Context 10 kb 10 kb ~30 kb short windows 1 Mb ~197 kb
Backbone dilated res-CNN dilated res-CNN res-CNN res-CNN U-Net + transformer multi-scale conv MetaFormer
Highest output level site site usage site usage junction junction transcript
Targets annotation RNA-seq usage RNA-seq usage annotation / alignments RNA-seq tracks usage$^{1/3}$ + long-read isoforms
Species human 4 8 human (+ others) human, mouse 10 (as input)
Tissue handling none output heads none none output tracks RBP-signature conditioning (fine-tune)
Structured output none none none pairwise pairwise splice graph + DP

From this, I see six recurring techniques.

12.1 Long context, cheaply

Every model grows the receptive field with an exponential mechanism: dilation, pooling, or both. Only AlphaGenome uses attention over the long axis, and only at reduced resolution. For splicing, local resolution matters more than global attention; the needed long-range signal is sparse.

12.2 Quantitative targets, reshaped

The move from annotation labels to RNA-seq usage was the first big step. The second was reshaping those targets (normalization by gene maximum, cube root) so that rare events carry gradient. Target engineering is as important as architecture.

12.3 Pairwise heads for junctions

Splam, AlphaGenome and SpliceAI2 all represent junctions as functions of two positions. SpliceAI2’s version (top-k candidates + bilinear Q·K with genomic RoPE) is a light, scalable way to do it.

12.4 Structured prediction on top of neural potentials

SpliceAI2 brings back the CRF/HMM view of gene structure, now with learned potentials and end-to-end training. This idea is also appearing in gene finding (Tiberius, Helixer). It turns a set of local scores into a globally consistent object.

12.5 Context as an input rather than a head

Species one-hot and RBP signatures both turn context into an input. This favours a shared code with context-dependent modulation, matching the biology of a common spliceosome tuned by trans-acting factors, and it allows counterfactual queries.

12.6 Careful variant scoring

A shared candidate set across alleles, ensemble averaging before selection, and simple max-delta summary scores matter as much as the model. The AlphaGenome configuration sweep shows how much a score definition can move a benchmark.

13. What is still missing

The SpliceAI2 discussion is candid about the gaps, and I think they define the next generation of models.

Context-dependent variant effects. Tissue-specific splicing is predicted, but tissue-specific variant effects are not, beyond baseline usage. Single-cell data and perturbation screens of splicing factors may provide the missing supervision, if the sparse junction coverage of single-cell data can be handled.

Beyond splicing alone. Transcripts are merged by intron chain, so transcription start and polyadenylation are ignored. Long reads make it possible to model splicing and 3’ end formation jointly, which the splice graph could naturally extend to with start and end nodes.

Kinetics and order. Splicing is co-transcriptional, and the order of intron removal and the elongation rate affect outcomes. Current models are static maps from sequence to steady-state usage. Data on splicing order and timing could turn them into kinetic models.

Mechanism. These models learn RBP motifs and branch point features, but the spliceosome itself remains a black box. In my CryoDRGN-AI post, I discussed how heterogeneous cryo-EM reveals the conformational landscape of the spliceosome. A long-term goal could be connecting the two worlds: sequence-to-splicing models that tell us what is spliced, and structural landscapes that tell us how the machine gets there.

Design. A differentiable model with a transcript likelihood is an attractive objective for RNA and DNA design: optimizing a sequence to favour a specific isoform, to rescue a mis-spliced exon, or to design splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides. The splice graph gives a natural reward: the log-probability of the desired transcript.

14. Conclusion

SpliceAI2 is less a new architecture than a careful integration of techniques that the field has been accumulating:

long context via dilation + multi-scale pooling
MetaFormer blocks with depthwise convolution
deep supervision through per-block heads
quantitative RNA-seq usage targets, cube-root transformed
massive multi-species data with species as input
pairwise junction head (top-k candidates, Q·K with genomic RoPE)
splice graph CRF with forward-algorithm training and Viterbi decoding
Muon + AdamW optimization, small ensemble
consistent variant scoring with shared candidates
tissue/disease conditioning on RBP expression (bi-FiLM, cross-attention decoder, difference loss)

Its main conceptual step is to treat the transcript as the prediction target, with an exact likelihood over an exponential space of isoforms, while still learning from abundant short-read data. Its main empirical lesson is that much of the gain comes from data scale and target design, especially from learning the long tail of rarely used splice sites, rather than from model size.

The broader trajectory is clear. Splicing models have gone from classifying positions, to quantifying sites, to pairing them into junctions, to assembling junctions into transcripts. The next step is probably to make these predictions context-aware and dynamic: in which cell, under which regulator state, at what time, and through which conformations of the spliceosome.

entry.title: CryoDRGN-AI: Notes on ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction and its implications for spliceosome dynamics

link.title: CryoDRGN-AI: Notes on ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction and its implications for spliceosome dynamics

entry.content:
Structural biology is increasingly moving beyond the idea of a single static structure. Many macromolecular machines do not exist in one dominant conformation. Instead, they occupy an ensemble of states. Ribosomes rotate, spliceosomes bend and remodel, molecular motors step through cycles, and membrane complexes assemble, disassemble, or shift between functional conformations.

This makes cryo-EM and cryo-ET reconstruction a natural machine learning problem. The question is no longer only:

What is the 3D structure?

but rather:

What is the distribution of 3D structures that explains the observed particle images?

The CryoDRGN series is important because it reformulates heterogeneous cryo-EM reconstruction as a generative modeling problem. Instead of assigning particles into a small number of discrete classes, CryoDRGN learns a continuous latent space where each point corresponds to a possible molecular state.

The 2025 CryoDRGN-AI work pushes this idea further. It moves from heterogeneous reconstruction with pre-estimated poses toward ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction, where both particle conformations and particle poses are optimized within a unified neural framework.

This post helps to learn the CryoDRGN series together with readers from a machine learning perspective, with emphasis on CryoDRGN-AI: its network architecture, forward model, loss design, and why these choices are well matched to structural heterogeneity. At the end, I discuss the spliceosome as an example of how latent structural landscapes can help us reason about dynamic molecular machines and also might help with RNA design.

1. Cryo-EM reconstruction as a Generative Modeling Problem

In single-particle cryo-EM, each observed particle image can be modeled as a noisy 2D projection of a 3D molecular volume:

\[I_i = \mathrm{CTF}_i \cdot \mathcal{P}_{R_i,t_i}(V_i) + \epsilon_i\]

where:

  • $I_i$ is the observed 2D particle image;
  • $V_i$ is the 3D density volume corresponding to particle $i$;
  • $R_i$ is the 3D orientation;
  • $t_i$ is the in-plane translation;
  • $\mathcal{P}_{R_i,t_i}$ is the projection operator under pose $(R_i,t_i)$;
  • $\mathrm{CTF}_i$ is the contrast transfer function;
  • $\epsilon_i$ is imaging noise.

For homogeneous reconstruction, all particles are assumed to come from the same structure:

\[V_i = V\]

The goal is then to estimate one consensus 3D density map.

However, this assumption is often too restrictive. Many biological complexes are heterogeneous. Different particles may correspond to different conformational or compositional states. In this case, it is more natural to write:

\[V_i = V(z_i)\]

Here, $z_i$ is a latent variable representing the structural state of particle $i$.

This is the key conceptual shift behind CryoDRGN:

Each particle is not merely a noisy view of one fixed volume.
Each particle is a noisy view of one point on a structural manifold.

2. CryoDRGN: A neural implicit representation of structural heterogeneity

CryoDRGN represents the heterogeneous 3D density field using a coordinate-based neural network. Instead of storing each volume as a voxel grid, it learns a function:

\[f_\theta(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}) \rightarrow \rho(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{z})\]

or, in Fourier space:

\[f_\theta(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{z}) \rightarrow \hat{\rho}(\mathbf{k};\mathbf{z})\]

where:

  • $\mathbf{x}$ is a real-space coordinate;
  • $\mathbf{k}$ is a Fourier-space coordinate;
  • $\mathbf{z}$ is a low-dimensional latent vector;
  • $f_\theta$ is a neural decoder, typically implemented as a multilayer perceptron;
  • $\theta$ denotes the shared decoder parameters.

This representation means that a 3D volume is not a fixed array. A volume is generated by querying the decoder at many spatial or Fourier coordinates under a given latent code:

\[\mathbf{z} \rightarrow V_\theta(\mathbf{z})\]

Different latent codes generate different structures:

\[\mathbf{z}_1 \rightarrow V_1,\quad \mathbf{z}_2 \rightarrow V_2,\quad \mathbf{z}_3 \rightarrow V_3\]

This design has several important implications.

First, the representation is continuous. The decoder can be queried at arbitrary coordinates, so the volume is represented as a continuous field rather than a fixed voxel array.

Second, the representation is generative. Sampling or interpolating latent variables generates new density maps along the learned structural landscape.

Third, the model directly couples representation learning with cryo-EM physics. The network does not simply reconstruct 2D images; it must explain 2D images through 3D density fields and projection operators.

3. Original CryoDRGN as a VAE-Like Model

The original CryoDRGN model can be understood as a variational autoencoder-like architecture.

An encoder maps each particle image to a distribution over latent conformational states:

\[q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_i \mid I_i) = \mathcal{N} \left( \mu_{\phi}(I_i), \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{\phi}^{2}(I_i)) \right)\]

A latent code is sampled from this approximate posterior and passed to the neural decoder. The decoder generates a 3D density volume conditioned on $\mathbf{z}_i$. This volume is then projected according to the particle pose and modulated by the CTF:

\[\hat{I}_i = \mathrm{CTF}_i \cdot \mathcal{P}_{R_i,t_i} \left( V_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_i) \right)\]

The training objective is based on the evidence lower bound:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}} = \sum_i \mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_i \mid I_i)} \left[ \log p_{\theta} \left( I_i \mid \mathbf{z}_i, R_i, t_i \right) \right] - \beta D_{\mathrm{KL}} \left[ q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_i \mid I_i) \parallel p(\mathbf{z}) \right]\]

Equivalently, as a minimization objective:

\[\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{VAE}} = \sum_i \left\| I_i - \hat{I}_i \right\|_2^2 + \beta D_{\mathrm{KL}} \left[ q_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}_i \mid I_i) \parallel \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) \right]\]

The reconstruction term comes from a Gaussian noise assumption. If the image noise is modeled as independent Gaussian noise, then maximizing the image likelihood is equivalent to minimizing squared reconstruction error.

The KL term regularizes the latent space. It encourages the posterior latent distribution to remain close to a simple prior, usually a standard Gaussian. This prevents the latent representation from becoming an arbitrary lookup table with no smooth global structure.

The parameter $\beta$ controls the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and latent smoothness.

4. Why CryoDRGN Is Not a Standard Autoencoder

A standard image autoencoder would learn:

2D image → encoder → latent code → decoder → reconstructed 2D image

CryoDRGN is different. Its decoder must generate a 3D molecular density:

2D image → latent code → 3D density → projection → reconstructed 2D image

The image reconstruction loss is therefore not merely a pixel-level autoencoding objective. It is a physics-constrained likelihood.

The model must explain each observed image through:

latent conformation
    ↓
3D density field
    ↓
pose-dependent projection
    ↓
CTF modulation
    ↓
predicted 2D particle image

This provides a crucial inductive bias. The network cannot freely memorize image-level statistics. It must explain all particles through a shared family of 3D structures.

This is why CryoDRGN is more than a neural image reconstruction method. It is a generative model constrained by cryo-EM image formation physics.

5. From CryoDRGN to CryoDRGN-AI

The original CryoDRGN framework usually assumes that particle poses are already known or estimated from an upstream pipeline such as RELION or cryoSPARC. In mathematical terms, it optimizes over the decoder and latent conformations while treating $R_i$ and $t_i$ as given:

\[\min_{\theta,\{ \mathbf{z}_i \}} \sum_i \left\| I_i - A_i \left( V_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_i); R_i, t_i \right) \right\|_2^2\]

Here, $A_i$ denotes the cryo-EM forward operator, including projection, CTF modulation, and image-space or Fourier-space sampling.

This assumption can become a bottleneck. If pose estimates are wrong, especially in highly heterogeneous or low-SNR datasets, the learned latent landscape may be distorted. Pose errors can be absorbed into the latent space, causing the model to confuse orientation uncertainty with structural variation.

CryoDRGN-AI addresses this problem by optimizing pose and conformation together:

\[\min_{\theta,\{\mathbf{z}_i\},\{R_i,t_i\}} \sum_i \left\| I_i - A_i \left( V_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_i); R_i, t_i \right) \right\|_2^2\]

This turns the problem into ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction. The model no longer relies on fixed upstream pose estimates. Instead, it learns:

global neural decoder parameters
particle-specific conformational latent codes
particle-specific orientations
particle-specific translations

within a unified optimization problem.

6. CryoDRGN-AI Uses an Autodecoder Architecture

A major architectural change in CryoDRGN-AI is the use of an autodecoder.

In the original VAE-style CryoDRGN, the latent code is inferred by an encoder:

\[z_i = E_\phi(I_i)\]

In an autodecoder, there is no encoder. Each particle has its own learnable latent code:

\[z_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\]

These latent codes are stored in a particle-indexed lookup table and optimized directly during training.

The model therefore contains two types of learnable variables.

Global parameters:

  • $\theta$: parameters of the neural decoder

Particle-specific parameters:

  • $z_i$: conformational or compositional latent code
  • $R_i$: particle orientation
  • $t_i$: in-plane particle translation

The forward pass can be summarized as:

particle index i
    ↓
retrieve z_i, R_i, and t_i
    ↓
query neural decoder f_θ at Fourier coordinates conditioned on z_i
    ↓
generate pose-dependent 2D projection
    ↓
apply CTF and translation phase shift
    ↓
compare predicted image with observed image

In formula form:

\[\hat{I}_i = A_i \left( f_\theta(\cdot,z_i),\phi_i \right)\]

where:

\[\phi_i=(R_i,t_i)\]

This autodecoder design is important because cryo-EM particle images are extremely noisy. Asking an encoder to infer a reliable latent code from a single low-SNR 2D image is difficult. Directly optimizing particle-specific latent codes can be more stable for reconstruction, even though it sacrifices the fast amortized inference provided by an encoder.

This is conceptually similar to neural implicit shape models such as DeepSDF, where each object has an optimized latent code and a shared decoder maps coordinates plus latent codes to shape values.

7. Fourier-Space Forward Model

CryoDRGN-style methods often operate naturally in Fourier space because of the Fourier slice theorem. The 2D Fourier transform of a projection corresponds to a central slice through the 3D Fourier transform of the volume.

For a 2D Fourier coordinate $\mathbf{k}_{2D}$, the predicted image can be written as:

\[\hat{I}_i(\mathbf{k}_{2D}) = C_i(\mathbf{k}_{2D}) \cdot f_{\theta} \left( R_i^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} k_x \\ k_y \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{z}_i \right), \qquad \mathbf{k}_{2D}=(k_x,k_y)\]

where $C_i$ is the CTF for particle $i$.

Translation in real space corresponds to a phase shift in Fourier space:

\[\hat{I}_i(\mathbf{k}) = C_i(\mathbf{k}) \cdot f_{\theta} \left( R_i^{-1}\mathbf{k}, \mathbf{z}_i \right) \cdot \exp \left( -2\pi \mathrm{i} \, \mathbf{k}^{\top}\mathbf{t}_i \right)\]

This formulation is powerful because the entire image formation process becomes differentiable with respect to:

decoder parameters θ
latent code z_i
orientation R_i
translation t_i

The model can therefore refine both structure and pose through gradient-based optimization once a sufficiently good pose initialization is available.

8. Loss Function: Why this objective makes sense

Assume the observed image is generated as:

\[I_i = \hat{I}_i + \epsilon_i\]

with Gaussian noise:

\[\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I})\]

Then the negative log likelihood is:

\[-\log p \left( I_i \mid \mathbf{z}_i,\phi_i,\theta \right) = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \left\| I_i-\hat{I}_i \right\|_2^2 + \mathrm{const}\]

This gives the basic reconstruction loss:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}} = \sum_i \left\| I_i - A_i \left( f_{\theta}(\cdot,\mathbf{z}_i),\phi_i \right) \right\|_2^2\]

However, reconstruction loss alone is not enough. If every particle has a free latent code, the model may use $\mathbf{z}_i$ to memorize noise, junk features, or pose errors. The latent space would then lose biological meaning.

A common solution is to place a Gaussian prior on the latent codes:

\[p(\mathbf{z}_i) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})\]

The negative log prior gives an L2 penalty:

\[-\log p(\mathbf{z}_i) = \frac{1}{2} \left\| \mathbf{z}_i \right\|_2^2 + \mathrm{const}\]

Thus, a simplified CryoDRGN-AI objective can be written as:

\[\mathcal{L} = \sum_i \left\| I_i - A_i \left( f_{\theta}(\cdot,\mathbf{z}_i),\phi_i \right) \right\|_2^2 + \lambda_z \sum_i \left\| \mathbf{z}_i \right\|_2^2 + \lambda_{\theta} \left\| \theta \right\|_2^2\]

9. Why Latent Regularization Is Essential

Without regularization, an autodecoder can become too flexible. Each particle could receive a latent code that explains not only true conformational variability but also noise, contamination, or reconstruction artifacts.

Regularization constrains the information stored in each latent code:

\[\mathbf{z}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\]

This encourages the model to encode only variation that is shared across many particles. In other words:

A structural feature should appear in latent space only if it helps explain population-level variation.

This is especially important for biological interpretation. A useful latent space should separate or organize molecular states, not merely index individual particle images.

The low-dimensional bottleneck plays a similar role. If $z_i$ has too many dimensions, the model may memorize particle-specific noise. If it has too few dimensions, the model may fail to capture important biological variation. The dimension of $z$ therefore controls the representational capacity of the structural manifold.

10. Pose Estimation: The key optimization challenge

The most difficult part of ab initio cryo-EM reconstruction is pose estimation.

The pose variable is:

\[\phi_i=(R_i,\mathbf{t}_i)\]

where $R_i$ lies on the rotation group $SO(3)$, and $\mathbf{t}_i$ is the in-plane shift.

Directly optimizing pose from random initialization is difficult because the loss landscape over rotations is highly non-convex. Many orientations can produce partially similar projections, especially when the data are noisy or the molecule has approximate symmetry.

CryoDRGN-AI therefore combines two strategies:

Stage 1: hierarchical pose search
Stage 2: stochastic gradient descent refinement

10.1 Hierarchical Pose Search

Hierarchical pose search performs a coarse-to-fine search over a discretized pose grid:

\[\phi_i^{*} = \arg\min_{\phi \in \Phi_{\mathrm{grid}}} \left\| I_i - A_i \left( f_{\theta}(\cdot,\mathbf{z}_i),\phi \right) \right\|_2^2\]

This stage is robust because it does not require a good gradient-based initialization. It can search broadly over orientation space.

However, pose search is computationally expensive, and its precision is limited by the grid resolution.

10.2 SGD-Based Pose Refinement

After hierarchical search provides a reasonable initialization, pose can be refined as a continuous variable:

\[\phi_i \leftarrow \phi_i - \eta \nabla_{\phi_i} \mathcal{L}\]

This gradient-based stage is more precise and efficient once the optimization has entered a good basin of attraction.

The overall strategy is therefore:

use search for robustness
use gradients for precision

This is one of the most important engineering and algorithmic choices in CryoDRGN-AI.

11. Why CryoDRGN-AI Is More Unified Than a Traditional Pipeline

A conventional cryo-EM workflow often separates the problem into multiple stages:

particle picking
    ↓
2D classification
    ↓
ab initio reconstruction
    ↓
homogeneous refinement
    ↓
heterogeneous refinement
    ↓
3D classification
    ↓
downstream analysis

Each stage compresses uncertainty into intermediate results. For example, once poses are estimated, downstream heterogeneity analysis may treat them as fixed.

CryoDRGN-AI instead places several unknowns into one optimization problem:

\[\min_{\theta,\{\mathbf{z}_i\},\{\phi_i\}} \sum_i \left\| I_i - A_i \left( f_{\theta}(\cdot,\mathbf{z}_i),\phi_i \right) \right\|_2^2 + \lambda_z \sum_i \left\| \mathbf{z}_i \right\|_2^2\]

From a probabilistic perspective, this resembles MAP estimation:

\[\max_{\theta,\{\mathbf{z}_i\},\{\phi_i\}} \sum_i \left[ \log p \left( I_i \mid \theta,\mathbf{z}_i,\phi_i \right) + \log p(\mathbf{z}_i) + \log p(\phi_i) \right]\]

It is not full Bayesian posterior inference, but it is more unified than a pipeline that fixes poses before modeling heterogeneity.

The model jointly learns:

what the structure looks like
how the structure varies
how each particle is oriented
which particles occupy which structural states

This is why CryoDRGN-AI is best viewed as an ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction framework rather than merely a downstream heterogeneity visualization tool.

12. Conformational and Compositional Heterogeneity

CryoDRGN-style models can represent both conformational and compositional heterogeneity.

Conformational heterogeneity refers to continuous structural motion, such as:

  • domain bending
  • subunit rotation
  • opening and closing
  • local flexibility

Compositional heterogeneity refers to the presence or absence of density, such as:

  • factor bound or unbound
  • ligand present or absent
  • subunit assembled or missing
  • RNA or protein segment ordered or disordered

Because the decoder generates a full density field conditioned on $\mathbf{z}$, both types of variation can be represented:

\[V_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}) = \text{density field conditioned on latent state } \mathbf{z}\]

In latent space, these patterns may appear differently:

  • continuous trajectory: conformational motion
  • separate cluster: compositional state
  • outlier cluster: broken or junk particles
  • branching manifold: multiple assembly or transition pathways

This is one of the main advantages of the method. The user does not need to predefine the number of structural classes. The model can discover continuous and discrete variation from the data.

13. The Inductive Biases Behind CryoDRGN-AI

CryoDRGN-AI works not simply because it uses a neural network, but because it combines several strong inductive biases.

13.1 Three-Dimensional Consistency

Every predicted 2D image must come from a 3D density field.

The model cannot explain images without constructing 3D molecular structure.

13.2 Shared Decoder

All particles share the same neural decoder:

different particles have different latent codes, but the mapping from latent space to density is shared.

This encourages a global structural manifold rather than unrelated per-particle reconstructions.

13.3 Low-Dimensional Bottleneck

Each particle state is represented by a low-dimensional latent code:

the latent variable should capture structural variation, not pixel-level noise.

13.4 Physics-Based Forward Model

Projection, rotation, translation, Fourier slicing, and CTF modulation are explicitly included.

the neural network is constrained by microscope physics.

13.5 Search Plus Differentiable Optimization

Hierarchical search provides robust pose initialization. SGD provides continuous refinement.

global search improves robustness, local gradient optimization improves precision.

Together, these biases make the model suitable for noisy, heterogeneous structural biology data.

14. Why the Loss Should Not Be Interpreted as Ordinary Image Reconstruction

At first glance, the reconstruction term looks like ordinary mean squared error:

\[\left\| I_i-\hat{I}_i \right\|_2^2\]

But this interpretation is incomplete.

A generic image model could reconstruct each 2D particle without ever learning a molecule. CryoDRGN-AI cannot do this, because the predicted image must be generated through:

\[\hat{I}_i = \mathrm{CTF}_i \cdot \mathcal{P}_{R_i,t_i} \left( V_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_i) \right)\]

Thus, image reconstruction is only the observable consequence of a deeper constraint: the model must explain all images as projections of a shared family of 3D structures.

This is the essential difference between a physics-informed generative model and a standard image autoencoder.

15. CryoDRGN, CryoDRGN-ET, and CryoDRGN-AI

The CryoDRGN series can be viewed as a progression.

15.1 CryoDRGN

Core problem:

given particle images and estimated poses, learn continuous structural heterogeneity.

Core model:

VAE-like architecture with a neural implicit 3D decoder

15.2 CryoDRGN-ET

Core problem:

extend heterogeneous reconstruction to cryo-electron tomography.

Core model change:

use subtomogram tilt-series observations to learn heterogeneous 3D density maps in situ.

CryoDRGN-ET is important because it brings neural heterogeneous reconstruction closer to the cellular environment, where molecules are observed in crowded and native-like contexts.

15.3 CryoDRGN-AI

Core problem:

perform ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction without relying on fixed upstream pose estimates.

Core model change:

autodecoder architecture
particle-specific latent codes
particle-specific pose optimization
hierarchical pose search
SGD pose refinement
physics-informed image likelihood

CryoDRGN-AI is therefore not merely another post-processing method. It is a more complete reconstruction model that jointly estimates structure, heterogeneity, and pose.

16. Spliceosome as a Case Study

The spliceosome is an ideal example for CryoDRGN-style modeling.

Splicing is not a single structural event. It is a sequence of RNA-protein rearrangements involving snRNP assembly, branch point recognition, splice-site positioning, catalytic activation, exon ligation, and disassembly.

The spliceosome therefore does not naturally fit into a small number of rigid structural classes. Even within one nominal biochemical state, such as the pre-catalytic spliceosome, particles may show bending, rotation, subcomplex rearrangement, and local density variation.

Traditional 3D classification faces a trade-off:

too few classes: continuous motion is oversimplified;
too many classes: each class has lower signal and noisier maps.

CryoDRGN-AI offers a different representation. Instead of asking which class each spliceosome particle belongs to, it asks where each particle lies in a learned structural latent space.

This latent space can reveal:

continuous conformational trajectories
separated compositional states
outlier particle populations
broken or junk particles
rare intermediate conformations

For pre-catalytic spliceosome data, CryoDRGN-AI demonstrates how a learned latent representation can recover continuous bending motion and separate abnormal particles into outlier regions of latent space. This is biologically meaningful because spliceosome function depends on coordinated structural rearrangements rather than a single static architecture.

17. Interpreting a Spliceosome Latent Landscape

Suppose each spliceosome particle receives a latent code:

\[\mathbf{z}_1,\mathbf{z}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{z}_N\]

Collecting them gives a latent matrix:

\[Z = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{z}_1^{\top} \\ \mathbf{z}_2^{\top} \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{z}_N^{\top} \end{bmatrix}\]

We can visualize this latent distribution using PCA, UMAP, diffusion maps, or graph-based trajectory analysis.

Then we can select representative latent points:

\[\mathbf{z}^{(1)},\mathbf{z}^{(2)},\mathbf{z}^{(3)},\ldots\]

and decode them into density maps:

\[V^{(j)} = V_{\theta} \left( \mathbf{z}^{(j)} \right)\]

If moving along one latent direction generates maps where the spliceosome gradually bends, then that direction may correspond to a major conformational coordinate.

In this sense, the latent space becomes a candidate reaction coordinate for structural dynamics:

  • latent direction
  • decoded density maps
  • interpretable molecular motion

However, interpretation must be cautious. A latent direction may mix several factors:

  • true conformational variation
  • compositional heterogeneity
  • pose uncertainty
  • particle quality
  • CTF-related artifacts
  • local flexibility
  • junk particles

18. From Spliceosome Dynamics to RNA Design

The long-term value of CryoDRGN-AI is not only reconstructing structures. It may help define design objectives for dynamic molecular systems.

For a static protein, the design objective is often to stabilize a target structure.

For a dynamic molecular machine such as the spliceosome, a more meaningful objective may be to shift the population from one conformational basin to another.

In latent-space terms, a perturbation changes the structural distribution:

\[\Delta p(\mathbf{z}) = p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathrm{perturbation}) - p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathrm{control})\]

This provides a quantitative way to describe how a mutation, small molecule, antisense oligonucleotide, or RNA sequence change alters a molecular ensemble.

18.1 Stabilizing Specific Spliceosome States

If a latent region corresponds to a stalled, inactive, or pre-catalytic spliceosome state, one could imagine designing perturbations that increase the occupancy of that region:

\[\max_{\mathrm{design}} \Pr \left( \mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}_{\mathrm{target}} \right)\]

This design goal is ensemble-based rather than structure-based. The objective is not merely to bind a pocket, but to reshape the conformational population.

18.2 Connecting RNA Sequence to Structural State Distribution

Splicing regulation is strongly sequence-dependent. Mutations near splice sites, branch points, polypyrimidine tracts, or regulatory motifs may alter spliceosome assembly and activation.

A future experimental-computational pipeline could look like:

RNA sequence perturbation
    ↓
cryo-EM or cryo-ET data collection
    ↓
CryoDRGN-AI latent landscape
    ↓
population shift analysis
    ↓
connection to splicing outcome

This would make it possible to ask whether a sequence perturbation changes not only the final splicing product, but also the distribution of structural intermediates.

18.3 Designing Dynamic Function Instead of Static Stability

For molecular machines, flexibility is often functional. A useful intervention may need to preserve one motion while blocking another.

Possible design objectives include:

preserve productive motion
block harmful transition
stabilize a transient intermediate
destabilize a nonproductive basin
increase occupancy of an active state

CryoDRGN-AI provides a way to measure whether such objectives are achieved at the structural ensemble level.

19. Limitations and Cautions

CryoDRGN-AI is powerful, but its outputs require careful interpretation.

First, the learned latent space is not unique. Different initializations, masks, regularization strengths, preprocessing choices, and pose parameterizations may affect the geometry of the latent representation.

Second, decoded intermediate maps need particle support. If a region of latent space contains few particles, the generated structure may reflect interpolation rather than a well-supported biological state.

Third, pose and conformation can be entangled. Even though CryoDRGN-AI jointly optimizes pose and conformation, some pose uncertainty may still leak into latent variables, especially in low-SNR or preferred-orientation datasets.

Fourth, latent outlier clusters may represent biologically meaningful rare states, but they may also represent junk particles, broken complexes, ice contamination, or other data-quality issues.

Fifth, density-level interpretation should eventually be connected to atomic modeling, biochemical perturbation, mutagenesis, functional assays, or orthogonal structural evidence.

20. Conclusion

The CryoDRGN series reframes heterogeneous cryo-EM and cryo-ET reconstruction as a problem in physics-informed generative modeling.

Original CryoDRGN introduced the core idea:

image encoder
    ↓
latent conformation
    ↓
neural 3D decoder
    ↓
projection and CTF
    ↓
image likelihood

CryoDRGN-AI extends this into ab initio heterogeneous reconstruction:

particle-specific latent code
    +
particle-specific pose
    ↓
shared neural implicit 3D decoder
    ↓
differentiable cryo-EM forward model
    ↓
physics-based reconstruction loss

Its main machine learning contributions are the combination of:

neural implicit representation
autodecoder latent optimization
learnable particle poses
hierarchical pose search
SGD pose refinement
Gaussian image likelihood
latent regularization
physics-informed forward modeling

For dynamic systems such as the spliceosome, this framework is especially compelling. It does not force particles into a small number of static classes. Instead, it learns a structural landscape where continuous motion, compositional variation, abnormal particles, and possible intermediate states can be studied together.

In the long term, this type of model may shift structural biology from determining individual structures toward measuring and designing structural distributions. For biological machines, that may be the more natural level of description: not one structure, but a landscape of possible states and transitions. This is especially relevant for RNA design, where the goal is often not only to design a sequence that folds into one target structure, but to design an RNA molecule whose ensemble, accessibility, interactions, and conformational switching behavior produce the desired function. In this view, CryoDRGN-style latent landscapes could provide structural feedback for designing RNAs that stabilize productive spliceosomal states, avoid nonproductive conformations, or tune the population balance between competing molecular states.

References

  1. Zhong, E. D., Bepler, T., Berger, B., and Davis, J. H. CryoDRGN: reconstruction of heterogeneous cryo-EM structures using neural networks. Nature Methods, 2021.

  2. Kinman, L. et al. Uncovering structural ensembles from single-particle cryo-EM data using cryoDRGN. Nature Protocols, 2023.

  3. Rangan, R. et al. CryoDRGN-ET: deep reconstructing generative networks for visualizing dynamic biomolecules inside cells. Nature Methods, 2024.

  4. Levy, A. et al. CryoDRGN-AI: neural ab initio reconstruction of challenging cryo-EM and cryo-ET datasets. Nature Methods, 2025.

  5. Plaschka, C., Lin, P. C., and Nagai, K. Structure of a pre-catalytic spliceosome. Nature, 2017.

  6. Nakane, T. et al. Characterisation of molecular motions in cryo-EM single-particle data by multi-body refinement in RELION. eLife, 2018.
